title: Held-out lag checks catch a phase-jump artifact but not periodic plaintext
statement: On three previously unused books, a fixed shortest-significant-lag search selects the planted period in all nine settings per book under clean cycling, 2% word-level character substitution and 1% step holds. With one phase jump it selects 130 instead of 131 in four cases; fixed-lag tests on the subsequent 4,000 ciphertext words do not confirm those four. However, a repeated ten-character plaintext with independently random row choices triggers and confirms the search in every run, so holdout confirmation does not establish a cyclic column schedule.
check: Calibrate against additional genuinely independent books and periodic, repeated-passage, nonperiodic correlated and adversarial plaintexts, row-table collisions, multiple noise levels and schedule changes. Test unknown periods outside the scanned range, several change-point times and partial or gradual shifts, and compare honest false alarm rates by independent text. Develop and benchmark an uncertainty-aware unknown-key decoder against known-column oracles before using period evidence to exclude any language or cipher family.
method: Freeze the P-J-032 exploratory rule before running these three books: on the first 4,000 ciphertext words, compute exact-word equality rates at lags 2–160, obtain the maximum equality rate on each of 49 global token shuffles, and choose the smallest lag whose add-one maximum-calibrated tail is <=.05. If no lag qualifies, report none. On the following 4,000 ciphertext words independently shuffle 49 times and test only the selected lag; this is a fixed-lag confirmation check, not a new scan. Both stages use exact word strings and independent seeded shuffles. The method was originally chosen after inspecting P-J-026’s pilot, so this follow-up tests a previously adaptive rule on new texts but is not an independently published preregistration.
cipher: Use hash-verified Hermes P.III table SHA-256 fe3f24a46dbc6b655eab8dbbd75addf84ee4a7dbd387ad802af75d02edfe5b4d. For each plaintext source (Augustine Confessiones, El conde Lucanor, Nibelungenlied), retain normalized table-alphabet characters, use the first 4,000 as a Markov reference and the next 8,000 as plaintext. For each requested period 10, 24 and 131 and seed 1103, 2207 or 3301, sample distinct table rows. Baseline advances cyclically once per character; noise2 substitutes one random lowercase character in 2% of ciphertext words; gap1 holds instead of advancing with 1% independent probability; phasejump makes one extra row advance at position 2,000; random selects rows independently. The separate Markov control samples characters from an add-one bigram trained on the source reference and selects rows randomly. A repeated 10-character uniformly sampled motif with random rows tests periodic plaintext confounding. Three seeds per book reuse each source passage and are not independent texts.
results_interpretation: For each of the three books and nine period/seed combinations, clean, noise2 and gap1 each recover all nine exact periods and confirm the selected lag on the later segment. Phasejump recovers 9/9, 6/9 and 8/9 by book; all four errors are lag 130 for true period 131, and none is significant on the later segment. No random-row historical or sampled Markov control produces a significant training lag. Every repeated-motif trial selects and confirms a lag even though rows are independently random. The repeat motif and cipher schedule are determined only by period and seed, so its nine period/seed cases are duplicated across the three book labels and must not be counted as 27 independent controls.
limitations: The exact 2% substitution and 1% hold scenarios are narrow, as are a single phase jump, three periods, three books and three row keys per period. Exact-word matching may be brittle under different transcription noise; a static subsequent segment cannot establish robustness under later changes. Random-row and Markov controls are not exhaustive, and the ten-character motif is deliberately artificial. Global shuffle destroys dependence and can produce false significance for structured plaintext, including after holdout confirmation. NumPy default_rng and Python random algorithms are version-dependent; full script and NumPy version are included. No period search gives an unknown-column key or plaintext recovery, and no manuscript or season-heldout data were measured.
